summary:
Sex between men ceased to be a criminal offence in Singapore when Parliament repealed Section 377A on 29 November 2022, in the same sitting as a constitutional amendment reserving to Parliament rather than the judiciary the power to define marriage. Same-sex relations are legal for men and women, and Reuters reported in June 2023 that the LGBT community felt safer in the wake of the repeal.

No form of same-sex relationship is recognised. Singapore recognises neither marriage, civil union nor domestic partnership between same-sex partners, and the Women's Charter precedent that a marriage not between a woman and a man is void leaves only heterosexual marriages recognised. Same-sex couples are consequently excluded from the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights and social security benefits available to married couples. In December 2018 a gay Singaporean man won a landmark appeal to adopt his son, fathered through surrogacy in the United States; in January 2019 Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee stated that the government does not support the formation of family units with children of homosexual parents through processes such as adoption and would seek to strengthen adoption laws. That commitment has not been made into law, and same-sex couples do not generally have their adoption of children recognised.

Legal gender recognition is available but difficult. The MPSC report of February 2025 identifies the process as carrying prohibitive cost because genital surgery is a precondition, and names discrimination, abuse and restrictions facing transgender students, employment-sector discrimination, and discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings that discourages transgender people from seeking care as the community's key challenges to health and well-being.

Statutory protection remains partial. The Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but gender identity and expression are not protected grounds, so LGBTQ+ workers remain outside its scope. Outright International's overview of Singapore, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTI organisations still cannot register, a structural gap that survives decriminalisation.

Expression remains regulated. A clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden lifestyles prompted calls for review in July 2025, with a former radio DJ and actor arguing that the grouping has no place in a post-377A Singapore. The media regulator limits the promotion or glamorisation of the homosexual lifestyle on television and radio, imposing higher age ratings (NC16, M18, R21) on productions depicting same-sex sexual activity; in 2019 the rapper Joshua Su withdrew from a TEDx radio talk after being asked not to make sensitive comments about his sexuality. Public-order provisions still reach conduct: Section 294 of the Penal Code covers obscene acts in public places with a maximum of three months' imprisonment, a fine or both, and gay men were charged with soliciting in 11 cases between 1990 and 1994, with fines of $200 to $500.

Toilet access is unsettled in practice. Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College of the National University of Singapore provide gender-neutral toilets for their students, but during Wikimania 2023 at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre (16 to 19 August 2023) the temporary conversion of a female toilet to a gender-neutral one drew public backlash, including threats of a boycott of the venue and petitions against the change. Pink Dot SG and the non-profit group Oogachaga responded that gender-neutral toilets complement gendered toilets rather than replace them.

The Singapore Prison Service reported on 15 November 2023 that 10 transgender inmates were then behind bars and that no cases of assault against them had been recorded, a rare official datum on trans prisoners. On health care, Health Minister Gan Kim Yong wrote in May 2020 that the Ministry of Health expects doctors to practise evidence-based best practice and to respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the recourse, though no such complaint had been received from self-declared LGBTQ patients in the preceding three years. In January 2006 the Ministry of Community Development, Youth and Sports granted S$100,000 to Liberty League, an ex-gay conversion-therapy organisation; activists pressured the group into returning the grant and it has been defunct since 2014.
tangentialFactors:
The Fun and Abusive Global Barometers country profile for Singapore scores the jurisdiction across unified gay and transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index for 2011 to 2024, covering de jure protections alongside lived experience; the individual scores are not reproduced here.

Pride expression continues despite the residual regulation: Pink Dot SG has been held annually since 2009, with record crowds of approximately 28,000 in recent years, and government representatives noted as far back as 2014 that gay bars and clubs operate in Singapore. Intrepid Travel's visitor-facing page describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene including gay-friendly bars and pop-ups alongside its own solo-travel and room-sharing guidance, which is operator framing rather than an assessment of legal risk.

Social attitudes are uneven. A 2021 TODAY Youth Survey found 80% of respondents willing to work with LGBTQ people, with 6% disagreeing; 75% willing to form close friendships, with 10% disagreeing; and 58% willing to accept LGBTQ family members, with 18% disagreeing. Media residue after decriminalisation and the 2006 public grant to a conversion-therapy organisation indicate institutional attitudes that outlast the 2022 repeal.
localsOnly:
Residents in employment have no statutory recourse on grounds of gender identity or expression: the Workplace Fairness Legislation is Singapore's first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it omits LGBTQ+ workers. Transgender residents face a legal gender recognition process conditioned on genital surgery and priced prohibitively, alongside the discrimination, abuse and restrictions affecting transgender students and the discrimination and harassment in healthcare settings recorded in the February 2025 MPSC report.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Singapore, which constrains resident organising, advocacy and service provision even after the repeal of Section 377A. Same-sex partners cannot obtain the healthcare benefits, inheritance rights or social security benefits that flow from marriage, and same-sex couples do not generally have adoption of children recognised.

Health care for transgender and other LGBTQ residents is shaped by the Ministry of Health's expectation, stated by Health Minister Gan Kim Yong in May 2020, that doctors practise evidence-based best practice and respect patients' preferences and circumstances including sexual orientation, with complaints to the Singapore Medical Council as the route of redress. Transgender prisoners are counted officially: the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates in November 2023 with no recorded assaults against them. Gender-neutral toilets are established on some campuses, at Yale-NUS College and Tembusu College, but public facilities remain contested.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the January 2019 undertaking by Social and Family Development Minister Desmond Lee to strengthen adoption laws has been drafted, tabled or enacted is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory records the statement and notes that it has not been made into law.

The outcome of the July 2025 calls for review of the radio broadcast code clause grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest is not sourced, so whether the clause stands or has been amended is unresolved.

The Fun and Abusive Global Barometers index values for Singapore are described but not enumerated in the inventory, so no de jure or lived-experience score can be quoted here. The cost figures for legal gender recognition are characterised as prohibitive in the MPSC report without a stated amount, and no post-2022 fee schedule is sourced.

The Singapore Medical Council complaint data cited by the Ministry of Health covers the three years to May 2020 only; no later complaint figures for LGBTQ patients are available, and the inventory does not source any enforcement action under Section 294 of the Penal Code after the 2022 repeal.
